hook: You know “Be still, and know that I am God”. But did you know it is spoken over raging nations and broken weapons?
story:
This psalm was not written for a quiet afternoon. It is a song for the day the ground gives way: “though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas”.

Almost five hundred years ago, between 1527 and 1529, the reformer Martin Luther turned it into a hymn. In English it is called A Mighty Fortress Is Our God, and it has been known ever since as the battle hymn of the Reformation.

That name fits the psalm. When God says “Be still”, he is not speaking into silence. He is speaking into the noise of nations and armies, and telling everyone within earshot who is God. The stillness his people find there is the stillness of a refuge in a storm.

moment:
This psalm is a song for a whole people to sing together, and for most of its length the singers do the talking: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.”

Then, near the end, the voice changes. God himself speaks, and he is not speaking only to the singers. He addresses the raging world around them: “I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted on the earth.” And the people answer with the line that closes the psalm: “The LORD of Armies is with us. The God of Jacob is our refuge.”
around: The verse before it describes what God does: “He makes wars cease to the end of the earth. He breaks the bow, and shatters the spear.” The psalm opens with the confidence it ends on: “God is our refuge and strength”.
readings:
For centuries believers have used this verse as a doorway into quiet prayer. They sit down, stop talking and remember who God is. Many have found in these few words a way into silence.

Read inside the psalm, the words are stronger than that. They are an order to a world at war to lay down its weapons and recognize its God. Some translations bring out that sense of stopping a fight.

The two belong together. The quiet a person finds in this verse is not the quiet of an empty room. It is the quiet of someone who has remembered, in the middle of the noise, who holds the nations.
argued:
In the eleventh century the great Jewish commentator Rashi read this verse as an order to armies. God speaks to the nations marching against his city: [[rashi]] Hebrew Bibles number the verse 46:11.

Six centuries later in Scotland, the Covenanter preacher Richard Cameron preached on these words in July 1680, days before he was killed at Airds Moss. The London preacher Charles Spurgeon kept one line from that sermon in his Treasury of David: [[cameron]]

Spurgeon himself heard the verse speaking to two audiences at once: [[spurgeon-psalm]]

And on September 11, 2011, ten years after the attacks, President Barack Obama read Psalm 46 at the new September 11 Memorial in New York, after a moment of silence at the minute the first plane struck.

An order to armies, a preacher days from his death, a word to enemies and believers, a nation remembering its dead: the stillness in this verse has never been an empty one.
point: “Be still” is first a command to stop fighting and to recognize who God is. The rest it gives his people follows from that: the one who ends wars is their refuge.
